meta.title: Alexis Sanchis - Software engineer, healthcare & security
meta.description: Software engineer working mostly on healthcare and home-care software, with a focus on security. In teams: a booking platform with 80,000+ users and offline-first apps for home-care nurses.

hero.bio: Six of my nine years in software went into healthcare and home care. I worked in the team behind a booking platform with 80,000+ users, and on offline-first apps for nurses working in areas with poor coverage. These days I build with agents, and I keep ownership of review and security.

items.title: Opaline Santé
items.problem: Let patients book home care with independent healthcare professionals (nurses, physiotherapists, etc.).
items.built: Fullstack developer in the Opaline Santé team. I also contributed to the shared UI component library with the design team. Stack: Next.js, Symfony, Laravel.

items.title: Offline-first apps for home care
items.problem: Home-care services (SSIAD, SAD), nursing homes (EHPAD) and meal-delivery teams often work where the mobile network is weak or missing.
items.built: Offline-first Android apps, built as a team: an embedded SQLite database on the device, synced with the server in the background. Stack: Java and Kotlin, later Flutter.
items.result: Care teams keep working without a connection, and their data syncs once the network is back.

items.title: Subscription platform for a speech therapist
items.problem: A speech therapist wanted to put her exercises online and offer them as a monthly subscription, to her patients and to anyone who wants to improve.
items.built: The whole platform, in under 24 hours of total work with agents. Stack: Next.js, Supabase, Stripe (subscriptions), Vercel.

items.title: Joinery application
items.problem: A complete joinery application that computes the overall performance of each product, such as Uw (thermal transmittance) and TL (light transmittance).
items.built: Built as a team: a joinery engine on the front end (React) and, on the back end (Django), an engine that computes the overall performance of each product (Uw, TL, etc.).

items.text: A WordPress site migrated to Next.js in under 45 minutes.
A few CLI tools in Rust.
Three Kotlin Android apps in closed testing on Google Play.

how.title: How I work with agents
how.intro: I use agents to move faster, but I'm still responsible for what ships: architecture, tests, security and maintenance.
how.setup: I build on [pstack](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack), Lauren Tan's open-source collection of skills for agents. I use an adapted version in Claude Code, with my own rules loaded in every session.

steps.name: Understand
steps.text: Before touching the code, the agent explains how that part works and why it was built that way, based on the code and its history.

steps.name: Design
steps.text: Types, signatures and module boundaries are set before implementation, so the structure can still be changed cheaply.

steps.name: Implement
steps.text: Only what was asked, with unit tests for the happy path, edge cases and errors. No extra features, no dead code.

steps.name: Verify
steps.text: “It compiles” is not enough: I want to see the feature running. A bug gets reproduced first, then fixed at the root. A performance gain is measured before and after.

steps.name: Review
steps.text: Before merging, the agent checks what the change could break outside the diff, by running the code. I make the final call.

rules: Every command, flag, package and version is checked against the official docs, with a source.
What is verified, what is assumed and what is uncertain are kept separate.
Infra commands get a dry run first, and the rollback is planned before the change.
Nothing destructive or touching production happens without my confirmation.
